description: ​We are team NEFRET.AI, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are developing "AstroResilience OS", an advanced system featuring a Smart Nutrition Tagging System and on-device security architecture for astronaut biometrics and health monitoring. Our team is fully assembled, and we are working together to bring this innovative solution to life for space exploration.
summary:
AstroResilience OS is an offline health-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions such as a journey to Mars, where messages to Earth can take up to 24 minutes each way and the link can drop. Instead of waiting for advice from the ground, the astronaut gets help directly on the device.

The app reads vital signs from a smart-patch simulator (heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, skin temperature and activity). It runs an explainable edge engine that predicts five risks before they cross a danger threshold: fatigue, physiological stress, hypoxia, thermal stress and nutrition deficit. Every alert explains why, and is linked to NASA's spaceflight hazards and Human Research Program risks. The app then recommends a concrete action and suitable space foods, logs what the astronaut actually ate, and learns two things over time: the astronaut's personal baseline and which foods they really finish.

All data stays on the device, encrypted with AES-256, with no network, backend or login. This matters because future crews will need to manage their own health on their own. AstroResilience doesn't just monitor: it predicts, recommends, and learns.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AstroResilience OS is an offline health assistant for astronauts on long missions, such as a trip to Mars. Messages between Mars and Earth take 4 to 24 minutes each way, and the link can drop, so the crew can't wait for advice from the ground. Our app runs fully on the astronaut's device and works like a small medical console that is always on.

HOW IT WORKS: 5 LAYERS

1. Telemetry Simulator: a simulated smart patch sends heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen (SpO2), skin temperature and activity every 2 to 10 seconds. Six live scenarios (Nominal, Fatigue onset, Hypoxia event, Thermal stress, Nutrition deficit, Recovery) change the vitals smoothly over 90 seconds, with realistic sensor noise. A Replay source can also play a real data file with no code changes. The included sample file is simulated and labeled that way.

2. Edge AI Engine: an explainable, rule-based engine looks at the last 12 readings. It detects five risks: fatigue, physiological stress, hypoxia, thermal stress and nutrition deficit. It fits a trend line to predict how many minutes are left before a threshold is reached, and raises an early "WATCH" alert before any limit is crossed. It produces a 0-100 risk score, and every prediction lists the exact signals behind it. It learns each astronaut's personal baseline from calm readings only, so an illness is never learned as "normal".

3. Predictive Nutrition Loop: for each risk the app recommends an action (rest, hydrate, reduce activity, breathing protocol) and ranks space foods inspired by ISS menus. The astronaut logs how much they ate (100/75/50/25%). The energy balance then updates, and the engine reacts on the next readings. Foods the astronaut usually leaves unfinished move down the list next time.

4. Offline Dashboard: Mission, Vitals, Nutrition and Mission Log tabs, plus a Demo Control screen.

5. On-device Security: logs are encrypted with AES-256, and the key is kept in secure storage. There is no network, no backend and no login. The astronaut can wipe all local data at any time.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- It warns early and explains why, instead of only showing raw numbers.

- It turns an alert into a concrete action the astronaut can take right away.

- It adapts to each astronaut and to their real eating habits.

- It keeps sensitive health data private on the device.

- The full log exports as JSON for the flight surgeon once the link to Earth returns.

The goal is to help future crews manage their health on their own, and the same idea fits remote places on Earth, such as polar stations, ships and rural clinics.

CREATIVITY

- The app predicts problems and gives the reasoning, so there is no black box.

- It closes the loop from measuring, to predicting, to recommending, to acting, to learning.

- It connects health monitoring with nutrition and energy balance.

- Each risk is linked to NASA's spaceflight hazards and related Human Research Program risks, and a References screen shows the NASA and CSA sources we used.

- The "Pressure Suit" design uses International Orange, the color of launch-and-entry suits: the system protects the astronaut the way the suit does.

TOOLS

- Flutter and Dart, for Android and web

- provider, fl_chart, hive_ce (encrypted storage), flutter_secure_storage, uuid, intl

- IBM Plex fonts, bundled with the app

- GitHub and GitHub Actions to build the Android APK automatically

- Chrome DevTools for testing

- 84 automated tests

Hardware: no physical sensors. Vital signs are simulated, and the app was tested on Android phones and in Chrome.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Communication delay and link loss, which is why everything runs offline.

- Explainability for medical decisions.

- Avoiding false alarms: we use smoothing, sustained readings, combined signals and trend checks.

- Privacy of health data.

- A clear, accessible interface: status is always shown with an icon and text, never color alone.

- Honesty about data: telemetry is simulated, thresholds are general physiology values rather than NASA flight rules, and food values are approximate.

Next steps: real wearable input, radiation dose monitoring, multi-crew support, and syncing with Earth.
